name: Canoe carriage at Vaiala
origin: Vaiala, Samoa, as depicted
dateKind: La Farge made this watercolour in 1891.
evidence: In John La Farge’s watercolour, three figures are spaced along a canoe that they carry near the water in Vaiala.
limit: The painter’s view does not tell us the canoe’s weight or which person carried most of it.
altText: Three figures support a long green canoe beneath trees.
stake: The rack keeper wants the long parcel to arrive with both handles where a short carrier can reach them.
change: A wet canvas wrap adds weight to the right end overnight.
axleResult: The long parcel stays tied at its wide rings. The keeper moves the rack stop and checks both handles again.
tieResult: The keeper adds a nearer right ring. The axle mark stays readable, and one strap now runs farther in.
originalTitle: Girls Carrying a Canoe, Vaiala in Samoa
medium: Watercolor, gouache, and graphite on off-white wove paper

name: Buildings at Akaroa
origin: Akaroa, Te Pātaka o Rākaihautū / Banks Peninsula, as depicted
dateKind: The print is dated 1860. The catalogue title gives 1845 for the view.
evidence: Charles Meryon’s 1860 etching depicts buildings at Akaroa. The scene carries the earlier date 1845 in the collection title.
limit: The later etched view does not supply measurements for any doorway or floor.
altText: A group of long, low buildings sits below trees and a hill.
stake: The porter needs an adjustable setting before the next tightly wrapped bundle comes out of the store.
change: The folded covering stays outside today. The keeper parks the same right bundle on the outer ring so a visitor can lift their lid.
axleResult: The old ring spacing stays available. A moved stop takes a fresh axle mark.
tieResult: The right bundle moves to the inner ring, letting its loose strap clear the apron string.
originalTitle: Native Barns and Huts at Akaroa, Banks Peninsula, 1845, from "The Voyage to New Zealand (1842–46)"
medium: Etching

name: The Pilot of Tonga print
origin: Tonga in the title of a French print
dateKind: The catalogue dates this two-plate print to 1855.
evidence: Meryon made this Tonga-titled etching using two plates with black and red ink. The sheet includes lines of verse.
limit: The print gives a composition and a story. It does not identify current terms for a port handover.
altText: An ornamental band surrounds lines of verse in two inks.
stake: The Cart Bay has two tied packets for one audience. The rail keeper needs their straps to stay separately marked.
change: Two proofs are added to the right-hand packet before handoff.
axleResult: The keeper shifts the stop while both packet cords keep their separate marks.
tieResult: A new inner tie keeps the revised packet where the next reader can reach it.
originalTitle: The Pilot of Tonga, from "The Voyage to New Zealand (1842–46)"
medium: Etching (from two plates) printed in black and red ink

name: Sail under way in Meryon’s print
origin: The historical title says Îles Mulgrave
dateKind: This plate is an 1866 etching and drypoint in a series titled for the 1842–46 voyage.
evidence: Meryon’s narrow print shows a pointed sail and the visible side of a vessel above lines of text.
limit: The image gives one view of the sail. The two sides and any loaded depth remain outside it.
altText: A tall sail and low vessel appear above lettering.
stake: A learner at the rail has room to unfold the model once. The spare pieces travel in a separate bag.
change: A second shallow frame is packed with the right bag.
axleResult: The rack takes a revised axle slot. The folded sail and the frame stay apart.
tieResult: The frame bag pulls inward under a short strap. The paper sail keeps its own marked place.
originalTitle: Pro-Volant des Iles Mulgrave, from "The Voyage to New Zealand (1842–46)"
medium: Etching and drypoint

name: Portrait of Queen Emma’s party
origin: Queen Emma of Hawaiʻi and party, as identified in the photograph title
dateKind: This is the Met’s date for Gardner’s photograph, 1865.
evidence: Alexander Gardner’s group photograph places one seated person among three people who stand. The museum title names Queen Emma and her entourage.
limit: This photograph records a pose. It does not give the order of a procession or what its subjects carried.
altText: Four people pose against a plain background, one seated and three standing.
stake: The desk puts one sleeve per support. A helper must keep the labels tied to the right sleeves when they move.
change: The printed credit and a spare backing board go in the right sleeve.
axleResult: Both sleeves stay spaced. A new axle stop keeps their tabs on the aisle side.
tieResult: The right sleeve moves inward under its credited tab. The desk keeps the larger support separate.
originalTitle: Queen Emma of Hawaii and Her Entourage
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative

name: Wailuku at Hilo, seen by Gordon-Cumming
origin: Hilo, Hawaiʻi, Wailuku River as named by the Met
dateKind: The catalogue dates this work November 18, 1879.
evidence: Constance Frederica Gordon-Cumming painted a watercolour of the Wailuku at Hilo. The sheet shows pale water across a bed broken by dark rocks.
limit: The sheet conveys a view and a date. It provides no readings for the water or a current crossing.
altText: White water threads between dark rocks and green banks.
stake: A carrier has room for a long river sheet and a smaller tray of location clips.
change: The pad holder is left at the bench. The right tray comes back at the inner ring so the river-view sheet can open.
axleResult: The long sheet keeps its clear edge while the divider rides at a new axle stop.
tieResult: The right tray goes inward and its divider stays clipped. The outer ring is free for the wider sheet.
originalTitle: Hilo, Banks of the Wailuku, Hawaii
medium: Watercolor over graphite, heightened with white gouache

name: The ʻUvea fishing view
origin: ʻUvea, Wallis, as named in the print title
dateKind: The etching is dated 1863. The catalogue gives 1845 for the fishing view.
evidence: Charles Meryon’s long etching depicts fishing near low palm-covered islands. The collection title names ʻUvea and gives 1845 for the scene.
limit: The print’s scene and later making date serve different uses. The image gives no depth or size measures.
altText: Thin low islands and palms run across a wide band of water.
stake: Essi needs the long strip to reach the rail without winding the source tabs around it.
change: The right sleeve now holds a second paper tab for the date of the print.
axleResult: The long band stays spread across its two supports. A changed stop makes room for the new tab.
tieResult: A tab goes under the inward tie. Both dates remain visible when the carrier is parked.
originalTitle: Océanie: Îlots à Uvea (Wallis): Pêche aux Palmes, 1845 (Oceania: Fishing, near islands with palms in the Uea or Wallis Group, 1845), from "The Voyage to New Zealand (1842–46)"
medium: Etching with drypoint

name: Red Jacket off Cape Horn
origin: Cape Horn on an Australia-to-Liverpool route named in the print
dateKind: The lithograph dates to 1855. Its title names an August 1854 passage.
evidence: The Red Jacket lithograph shows the ship among ice. The printed legend names its route. Charles Parsons is credited on the stone.
limit: It depicts one part of a journey. Cargo weight and wind speed are absent.
altText: A sail ship passes pale floating ice above a route legend.
stake: The first route strip needs a stiff sleeve with its dates apart. Hale keeps a second slot open for a later account.
change: The right-hand box gains two stiff slip boards for the printed route.
axleResult: A fresh mark leaves both long sleeves on separate rings.
tieResult: The bulky board moves inward. The earlier passage date still sits beside the printed edition date.
originalTitle: Clipper Ship "Red Jacket" – In the Ice off Cape Horn, on Her Passage from Australia, to Liverpool, August 1854
medium: Hand-colored lithograph

name: Ferry crossing the Rokugō River
origin: Rokugō River, Japan, as depicted
dateKind: The Met dates this print to about 1834.
evidence: In Utagawa Hiroshige’s woodblock print, people share a low ferry moving between two banks.
limit: The composition shows a crossing. Neither a timetable nor a boat capacity follows from it.
altText: A ferry at mid-river with a busy bank behind it.
stake: The route keeper wants both banks reachable without switching the labels between them.
change: A padded stand is added to the right-hand bank model.
axleResult: The two banks keep their spacing. A yellow stop marks the reassigned axle position.
tieResult: The model of the right bank moves closer in, leaving room at the outer ring for its stand.
originalTitle: Ferry Boat Crossing the Rokugo River
medium: Woodblock print; ink and color on paper

name: The waterwheel at Onden
origin: Onden, Japan, as depicted
dateKind: The catalogue dates the print to about 1830–32.
evidence: Katsushika Hokusai placed a large waterwheel next to working figures in his print of Onden.
limit: The print gives apparent positions. It lacks readings of flow, speed or force.
altText: A wheel fills the left side while workers and Mount Fuji appear beyond.
stake: A helper needs the wheel mock-up and its fitting kit to stay separated on the cart.
change: The right fitting box gains a wooden hub for the morning lesson.
axleResult: The kit stays out at its marked ring. The wheel’s axle stop gets a second mark.
tieResult: The kits sit closer to the middle. The big mock wheel stays at the end where it clears the tray.
originalTitle: The Waterwheel at Onden (Onden no suisha), from the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (Fugaku sanjūrokkei)
medium: Woodblock print; ink and color on paper

name: Landing-stage in the snow
origin: A snow-covered landing-stage, Japan, in the print
dateKind: The print is dated 1800 in the Met catalogue.
evidence: Kitagawa Utamaro’s narrow woodblock print shows figures at a landing-stage as snow falls.
limit: The surface is part of the scene. The print does not test how much a rack or landing can hold.
altText: A tall narrow view shows figures and landing-stage rails in snow.
stake: One visitor will reach the bench before the rail group. The packet needs a strap they can reach alone.
change: The right packet comes back with a thick cloth cover against the snow.
axleResult: The current tie still fits the covered packet with a second axle stop.
tieResult: The covered parcel moves inward. The new strap can open without reaching across the rail.
originalTitle: Landing-stage in the Snow (Yuki no sanbashi)
medium: Woodblock print; ink and color on paper

name: Weighing Books
origin: China, Ming dynasty as catalogued
dateKind: The catalogue dates this hanging scroll to the early 16th century.
evidence: Guo Xu’s hanging scroll depicts weighing books. The museum records ink and colour on silk and gives separate image and mounted dimensions.
limit: The scroll offers a depiction. It supplies neither a reading for the books nor one for its hanging mount.
altText: A dark, tall silk composition shows people within the scroll mount.
stake: The Hall has a stack of mounted examples and a box of tags. Visitors should be able to compare mount and image separately.
change: The tags weigh the same. The mount comparison needs room at the centre, and the keeper parks the right-hand tag box at the outer ring.
axleResult: The image stays apart from the mount and the stop moves on the test board.
tieResult: The tag box pulls inward. There is room at the outer ring for the mounted example.
originalTitle: Weighing Books
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
dimensions: Image: 48 3/8 x 28 in. (122.9 x 71.1 cm) Overall with mounting: 103 x 34 1/8 in. (261.6 x 86.7 cm) Overall with knobs: 103 x 38 3/8 in. (261.6 x 97.5 cm)

name: An imperial carriage in one triptych sheet
origin: Japan, Meiji period
dateKind: The museum dates this sheet 1889.
evidence: Utagawa Kunitoshi’s 1889 carriage image is one sheet of a triptych. The scene includes the large carriage against a crowd.
limit: A single sheet has edges. It cannot show everything the missing companion sheets or surrounding street might have shown.
altText: A red carriage and horses fill a horizontal crowd scene.
stake: Only one part of the picture will sit on each mat. The receiver wants to leave spaces for the rest.
change: The spare mats stay in the store. The right parcel moves in one ring to clear a visitor’s turning space.
axleResult: The spacing between the mats stays fixed. The keeper shifts the underside stop.
tieResult: The unprinted mats move in, leaving the opening for the original single sheet at its ring.
originalTitle: Illustration of the Imperial Carriage (Gohōren no zu)
medium: One sheet of a triptych of woodblock prints; ink and color on paper

name: Steam locomotive at Takanawa
origin: Takanawa, Tokyo, as depicted
dateKind: The museum dates this triptych to about 1873.
evidence: Utagawa Kuniteru’s three-panel print depicts a steam locomotive running at Takanawa. The picture crosses sheet joins.
limit: A view made to be seen across three sheets does not establish train length or track clearance.
altText: A long train crosses the coloured panels beside open water.
stake: A learner folds the middle image over the other two to carry the set and needs its return side marked.
change: A longer divider is clipped to the right strip case.
axleResult: The strips keep their visible order across the rings and the stop moves underneath.
tieResult: The divider case moves inward. The pictures can still be laid out in order after delivery.
originalTitle: Illustration of a Steam Locomotive Running on the Takanawa Railroad in Tokyo (Tōkyō takanawa tetsudō jōkisha sōkō no zu)
medium: Triptych of woodblock prints; ink and color on paper

name: Loading cargo at Yokohama
origin: Yokohama, Japan, as depicted
dateKind: The museum dates this five-panel print to the fourth month of 1861.
evidence: Utagawa (Gountei) Sadahide made this five-part print of cargo loading. One view shows a sloped access board beside rigging and cargo.
limit: This image shows activity at a route edge. Package weight, who authorised a load and the order of all tasks are outside the image.
altText: Ropes, boxes, people and a diagonal access board fill the port picture.
stake: Rail helpers will lay out the access board after the cargo stand reaches them. They need to know which marks were checked empty of obstructions.
change: A wrapped spacer is added to the right-hand gangway model.
axleResult: Both gangway rails keep their broad footing. A changed notch is entered at the rack.
tieResult: The heavier end comes inward without covering the model’s access marks.
originalTitle: “Yokohama Trade: Westerners Loading Cargo”
medium: Pentaptych of woodblock prints; ink and color on paper

name: Market porter photograph
origin: Japan, photographer credited by the Met
dateKind: The museum dates this hand-coloured print 1865–1870.
evidence: Renjō Shimooka’s photograph shows a market porter carrying a pole with items suspended from it.
limit: The pose shows the relation of carried objects. The photographer does not give the load of each parcel or a testimony from the worker.
altText: A standing person holds a shoulder pole with bundles hanging at both ends.
stake: The next carrier wants to try a changed hanging point before the rail opens to more readers.
change: The keeper stuffs a second string of practice tags in the right bag.
axleResult: The bags keep their spacing on the model pole. The axle stop now has a fresh shoulder mark.
tieResult: The tag bag comes in one ring. The left bag stays ready to be counted where it began.
originalTitle: [Market Porter]
medium: Albumen silver print with applied color

name: A posed carriage photograph
origin: Japan, as catalogued for the photograph
dateKind: The Met dates this print to the 1870s.
evidence: In Suzuki Shin’ichi’s hand-coloured photograph a seated figure and a cane-backed carriage form part of the setting.
limit: A photograph of one pose does not show who usually rode, who pulled the vehicle or the route taken.
altText: A figure sits in a small carriage near a wall and two large wheels.
stake: A learner needs a separate parcel for the backrest and the paper with its source. Both should reach the counter in one trip.
change: An extra protection block is fitted in the right parcel.
axleResult: The backrest stays strapped at its widest spacing. The keeper adds a second notch mark.
tieResult: The right parcel uses the inner ring; the larger backrest still clears the edge of the cart.
originalTitle: [Japanese Woman in Carriage]
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative with applied color

name: The Harlem Railroad tunnel view
origin: Harlem, New York, as depicted
dateKind: The gouache is dated about 1837 by the Met.
evidence: Nicolino Calyo framed the tunnel area with a high building and a hillside in this Harlem Railroad view.
limit: The painter’s view supplies some visible relations. It does not establish surveyed clearance inside the cut.
altText: A large building rises above a dark rail cutting and foliage.
stake: Time Hall is setting aside a practice section for a visitor who wants to compare the unseen lining with the open entrance.
change: The same lining insert comes back. The next demonstration uses a narrower rack, bringing the right block in by one ring.
axleResult: A corrected axle mark keeps both sections available at their wide distance.
tieResult: The lining block pulls in towards the stop, so the open entrance block has its edge free.
originalTitle: View of the Tunnel of the Harlem Railroad
medium: Gouache on off-white wove paper

name: The Third Avenue Railroad Depot
origin: New York City, as depicted
dateKind: The painting dates to about 1859–60.
evidence: William H. Schenck’s painting gives the depot a long street frontage along the foreground route.
limit: The view relates a frontage to its street. It leaves the inside loading space unspecified.
altText: A brick depot spans the image beside a broad open street.
stake: The low bench wants a single trial position with room to read the frontage and street as separate routes.
change: The right-hand depot block picks up a second entrance tab.
axleResult: A second axle setting stays under the same long depot mock-up.
tieResult: The depot tabs move one ring inwards. The street strip remains flat on its end of the tray.
originalTitle: The Third Avenue Railroad Depot
medium: Oil on canvas

name: Baltimore & Ohio Railroad soup plate
origin: Made in England for the American market, per the Met
dateKind: The collection gives about 1828 to about 1846 for making the dish.
evidence: Enoch Wood & Sons put a railroad scene on this transfer-printed earthenware. The depot view lives within a circular border.
limit: The pottery received the railway image on a dish. Its diameter does not measure the width of the pictured rails.
altText: A dark scene of rail movement sits inside a circular patterned border.
stake: Two practice trays have different sleeve widths. The keeper wants the rim and printed scene treated as separate records.
change: The spare sleeve is loaned separately today. The filled right box sits one ring farther out to leave room for the round sample.
axleResult: Both tray spacers keep their full span. The axle now uses another marker.
tieResult: The filled sleeve moves inward and the outside ring can hold an empty round spacer.
originalTitle: [Baltimore & Ohio Railroad]
medium: Earthenware, transfer-printed

name: The Garbage Cart street view
origin: An American street scene, catalogue attribution
dateKind: The Met dates Chappel’s painting to the 1870s.
evidence: William P. Chappel’s street painting makes a single garbage cart part of a much wider street view.
limit: The date belongs to the painting. The view cannot give each worker’s route or the mass of the collected material.
altText: Small figures and carts appear among paved streets and low buildings.
stake: The street crew comes between shifts. The model boxes should leave a space for a spare clip to travel with the handover.
change: The right-hand box comes back with extra tags, still inside the same shape of lid.
axleResult: The lid lies between the same clips. The mark moves underneath the cart.
tieResult: The heavier tag box uses the inner ring. A spare clip can stay at the outer end for the whole shift.
originalTitle: The Garbage Cart
medium: Oil on slate paper

name: Winter Scene with Trestle Bridge
origin: Atlantic & Great Western Railway, as cited in the Met title
dateKind: The Met dates Ryder’s photograph 1862–64.
evidence: James Fitzallen Ryder photographed a railway trestle in a winter landscape. The near and far supports overlap in the image.
limit: The photograph shows a line of sight. It offers neither allowable loads nor a survey of every support.
altText: Dark trestle members stand behind snow and timber.
stake: The rail group wants to keep the near and far practice supports apart until everyone can see them.
change: A bundle of short feet for the bridge stand goes in the right box.
axleResult: The trestle’s two demo stations stay spaced apart under the changed stop.
tieResult: The feet move to the inner ring; the far support keeps its clear outer line.
originalTitle: [Winter Scene with Trestle Bridge Along the Atlantic & Great Western Railway]
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative

name: Algiers–Constantine railway opening medal
origin: Algiers and Constantine in the event title, Roty credited as French
dateKind: This struck medal is dated 1886. Its title identifies the opening on November 3 of that year.
evidence: Louis-Oscar Roty’s medal commemorates the opening of a line between Algiers and Constantine. The catalogue records bronze with silvering.
limit: The medal makes a commemoration visible. It cannot verify rail capacity or reflect every view of the opening.
altText: A round medal shows a figure and lettering in relief.
stake: Readers at the Hall need a cover tab that travels with the engraved event date and a model disc that can remain out.
change: A second blank disc is put in the right-hand rehearsal sleeve.
axleResult: Both disc positions stay open. A new stop accepts the fuller sleeve.
tieResult: The two discs share the nearer ring while the event-date tab stays in the deposit clip.
originalTitle: Opening of the Railway Line Between Algiers and Constantine, November 3, 1886
medium: Bronze, struck, silvered

name: Building of the French Railways medal
origin: France in the subject, made in Geneva in the record
dateKind: This silver medal was made in 1842 according to the Met.
evidence: Jean-François-Antoine Bovy’s railway medal shows Louis-Philippe’s profile on its face. The title links the object to building the French railways.
limit: The medal documents a commemorative message. Views from railway workers are outside this object.
altText: A portrait in profile is surrounded by lettering along a circular rim.
stake: A visitor needs to turn two edge markers without losing the fitted place for their broad printed copy.
change: A batch of pre-cut edge tabs rides in the right sleeve.
axleResult: The wide copy stays at its old tie. The keeper makes a new axle stop underneath.
tieResult: The tab sleeve slides inward. There is room to turn either model card at the edge.
originalTitle: Louis-Philippe and Building of the French Railways
medium: Silver, struck

name: The pilot boat Wm. J. Romer
origin: Atlantic voyage to England named on the print
dateKind: The print and its stated departure both date to 1846.
evidence: Nathaniel Currier’s lithograph names the pilot boat Wm. J. Romer and Captain McGuire in a legend below the sailboat.
limit: The legend gives a departure. A named boat and captain do not by themselves give an independently recorded arrival.
altText: A sailboat crosses green-blue water above a printed legend.
stake: The keeper keeps the departure and arrival envelopes on separate rings, ready for different signatures.
change: A new envelope sleeve stiffens the pack on the right end.
axleResult: The two signature trays stay separate with a changed stop.
tieResult: The heavier envelope sleeve moves inward. One outer ring stays spare if a signed arrival turns up.
originalTitle: Extraordinary Express Across the Atlantic – Pilot Boat Wm. J. Romer, [commanded by] Captain McGuire, Leaving for England, February 9th, 1846
medium: Hand-colored lithograph

name: Transferring cable to Great Eastern
origin: Sheerness, England, in the museum title
dateKind: Dudley’s watercolour dates to 1865.
evidence: Robert Charles Dudley’s watercolour depicts a cable passing from the Iris to the Great Eastern. The two hulls take up much of the image.
limit: It shows a transfer relationship. The painting gives no measured force or continuous load history.
altText: Two large dark hulls fill the foreground, with the nearer vessel’s paddle housing visible.
stake: The crew needs the two model hulls close enough to show the handover while keeping their source tabs separate.
change: A coil of demonstration string is added to the right-hand ledge.
axleResult: The hull models hold their spacing, with the heavier practice coil tested at a revised stop.
tieResult: The coil moves one ring inward. The two hull marks stay visible for the next demonstration.
originalTitle: The Old Frigate Iris with Her Freight of Cable Alongside the Great Eastern at Sheerness: The Cable Passed from the Hulk to the Great Eastern
medium: Watercolor over graphite with touches of gouache (bodycolor)

name: Figures Unloading Cargo
origin: French artist’s drawing, location unspecified in title
dateKind: The catalogue dates the drawing to the 19th century.
evidence: Pierre Puvis de Chavannes made this pen and ink drawing with multiple figures near boats and a cargo handover.
limit: The sheet sketches work and gestures. It does not identify those working or record wages or load weight.
altText: Fine ink strokes sketch people at a shore and boats beyond.
stake: The reader coming by the bench wants to place the light practice frame without disturbing the stack of dark backing paper.
change: The storage keeper adds a new stiff pad to the right pack.
axleResult: The frames keep their previous room to open. The mark moves along the cart below them.
tieResult: The right pack uses the inner ring. A reader can reach the sketched frame from beside it.
originalTitle: Figures Unloading Cargo from Sailing Vessels
medium: Pen and black ink, over black chalk, on beige paper.

name: Man Weighing Gold
origin: Netherlandish painter as catalogued
dateKind: The panel is dated about 1515–20.
evidence: Adriaen Isenbrant’s oil-on-wood picture shows a man holding a small balance in front of him.
limit: The painting depicts a balance and its holder. It does not give the instrument’s calibration or the tested weight.
altText: A man in a dark hat holds a fine balance against a dark background.
stake: A clerk wants people to compare the marked case and loose weights without treating either as a calibrated reference.
change: A heavy dummy cover has gone into the right box with the loose weights.
axleResult: The fitted axle moves while both reference rings keep their visible positions.
tieResult: The cover stays with the loose weights but moves one place inward, apart from the sealed left case.
originalTitle: Man Weighing Gold
medium: Oil on wood
dimensions: 20 x 12 in. (50.8 x 30.5 cm), with added strips of 1 3/4 in. (4.5 cm) at left and right

name: Boÿers (Dutch Cargo Ship)
origin: Dutch vessel in the title, Bohemian artist per the museum
dateKind: The etching is dated 1647 and identified as the first of two states.
evidence: Wenceslaus Hollar’s etching shows cargo vessels with tall rigging and smaller figures. The catalogue identifies this impression as the first state.
limit: A state of a print tells which version survives here. The visible ship forms do not give cargo weights.
altText: Tall rigging meets the top of an etched view above two hulls.
stake: The receiver checks two parts of the model at different heights. The trial should leave each part on its own checked ring.
change: The base plate stays with the other model. A broad aisle on the right closes, bringing the mast base carrier one ring in.
axleResult: The masts stay on their outer rests. The new axle stop accepts the added base plate.
tieResult: The heavier base goes inside one mark while the hull plate stays free to lift.
originalTitle: Boÿers (Dutch Cargo Ship)
medium: Etching; first state of two

name: Weighing
origin: British print by Rowlandson and publisher S. W. Fores
dateKind: The catalogue dates the print January 1, 1799.
evidence: Thomas Rowlandson’s coloured etching and aquatint places a weighing activity in a crowded composition.
limit: A satirical scene can frame reactions as evidence of its story. The figures supply no even series of readings.
altText: A crowded colour print shows a public weighing scene.
stake: Essi wants space for two people at once. The extra picture support must leave the reading order visible.
change: An old proof arrives as a second mat in the right packet.
axleResult: The two demonstration mats stay separate. The notch moves on the guide rail underneath.
tieResult: The old proof rides closer to the middle. The newer mat keeps its own opening space.
originalTitle: Weighing
medium: Hand-colored etching and aquatint

name: A porter with a wagon
origin: Bologna in the print series, Italy
dateKind: This print is dated 1646 in the museum record.
evidence: Simon Guillain II etched plate 11 after a figure design credited to Annibale Carracci. The porter appears with a wagon.
limit: The authorship credits distinguish the etched plate from its source image. The porter’s work remains outside both credits.
altText: An etched figure stands near a wagon, with lines of lettering below.
stake: The next porter needs to recognise the two old grips as well as the place for a newer strap.
change: A spare grip is tied to the right bundle next to the model wheel.
axleResult: The grip and wheel stay at the outer ring. A changed axle notch takes their full weight.
tieResult: The grip pack moves towards the axle. The wheel stays visible above the old ring mark.
originalTitle: Plate 11: Porter with a wagon, from "Diverse Figure" (later known as "Arti di Bologna")
medium: Etching
dimensions: Height: 11 in. (28 cm) Width: 6 5/16 in. (16 cm)

name: The Pie Wagon
origin: Cleveland, Ohio, in the Cleveland Museum of Art record
dateKind: Gaertner painted the scene about 1926 according to the collection.
evidence: Carl Gaertner paints a Star Bakery delivery wagon with workers nearby. The museum describes it as part of a lunch break outside factories.
limit: The painting shows a gathered group. It does not say how long the workers had or how many deliveries came before them.
altText: People cluster around a small wagon in front of tall factories.
stake: A helper parks once for two trays and leaves the rope tied so the next group can lift either one.
change: More folded tray pads go into the right bag for the return visit.
axleResult: The delivered lunch trays stay apart. The whole load takes another axle notch.
tieResult: The pad bag shifts inward. Both trays keep clear handles near the edge.
originalTitle: The Pie Wagon
medium: oil on canvas

name: Harbour, Swansea, Wales
origin: Swansea, Wales, as photographed
dateKind: The Cleveland Museum of Art dates this print to 1855.
evidence: Alfred Rosling’s photograph holds large vessels, rigging and their relation to the Swansea waterfront in one view.
limit: This dated angle shows the harbour from one position. It gives no second view across the moored vessels.
altText: Several rigged vessels appear in a pale albumen photograph.
stake: A learner wants a position at the low bench to open the print without looking round a tall model mast.
change: The right-hand mast bag holds its new base board.
axleResult: The tall mast stays in its wide position. A fresh stop keeps space open at the print’s side.
tieResult: The mast base pulls to the inner ring. The viewer at the low bench can reach the print from the edge.
originalTitle: Harbour, Swansea, Wales
medium: albumen print from wax paper negative

name: Two Boats at the Harbor of Dieppe
origin: Dieppe, France, as depicted
dateKind: The Cleveland Museum of Art dates Delacroix’s watercolour to 1854.
evidence: Eugène Delacroix’s harbour sheet depicts two boats, each with visible rigging, in light pencil and watercolour.
limit: The sheet gives a pairing from one view. It does not contain complete plans for the two boats.
altText: Two lightly coloured boats sit above a pale band of water.
stake: The rail keeper lays out two frames side by side so a group can follow both sets of lines.
change: The right tray now includes a line card and a second layer of stiff backing.
axleResult: The two trays stay their full distance apart. The stop changes to hold the backing.
tieResult: The right tray pulls in one ring. The extra backing sits underneath without crossing to the other tray.
originalTitle: Two Boats at the Harbor of Dieppe
medium: watercolor and pencil on paper laid down on board

name: Hemlock Forest, Lehigh Valley Railroad
origin: Lehigh Valley Railroad, in Cleveland’s record
dateKind: The Cleveland Museum of Art dates this photograph to about 1895.
evidence: William H. Rau photographed the railroad between tall trees. The two lines of track converge in the distance within the image.
limit: Convergence in the photograph is a view from a point. It does not record track width far from the camera.
altText: Two bright tracks narrow into a distant point in a dark forest.
stake: The keeper wants to hold one near and one far model without letting the far label slip off during carriage.
change: The return rack is shorter. The same right-hand kit comes in one ring, with the distance label still attached.
axleResult: The sections keep their long spacing. The axle stop moves and the far label stays with its stands.
tieResult: The right-hand kit moves inward. The distance drawn in the reference photograph remains separately labelled.
originalTitle: Hemlock Forest, Lehigh Valley Railroad
medium: albumen print from wet collodion negative

name: Morning Haze in Chichester Harbor
origin: Chichester Harbour, England, as depicted
dateKind: The Cleveland Museum of Art dates Frank Short’s aquatint to 1922.
evidence: Frank Short’s aquatint shows a narrow dark shore or craft line in a very pale harbour view.
limit: A patch unclear in this print cannot establish whether a route was empty or obscured.
altText: Faint horizontal marks stretch across pale water beneath the haze.
stake: A reader needs to move two light sleeves between the window and the bench, with their edges still obvious.
change: A second light diffuser has been packed in the right sleeve.
axleResult: A new stop preserves the carriers’ width while their sleeve edges remain visible.
tieResult: The diffuser sleeve goes in one ring. The clear outer mark stays available as a starting point.
originalTitle: Morning Haze in Chichester Harbor
medium: aquatint
